paras: The lynching of Matias Salmon was the hanging of a Mexican man accused of murder by a vigilance committee or mob at Grantsville, Nevada, on the night of Saturday, January 29, 1881. Salmon had been arrested for killing a miner the day before, and he was taken from the officers holding him and hanged from the framework of a windmill. A brief telegraphic dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, while Nevada and California papers printed longer accounts that approved of the hanging.

According to the Bodie Free Press, as reprinted by the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, Salmon, also known as Matias Alcantar, was a "Mexican desperado" who had figured in two shooting affrays at Bodie and another at Aurora. The Reese River Reveille, quoted by the Gold Hill Daily News, gave Salmon's age as twenty-nine and his birthplace as Chihuahua, and said the man he was accused of killing was reputed to be his fourth victim. The Bodie paper's account of his past, by contrast, names no earlier killings.

On Friday morning, January 28, Salmon was accused of killing a miner whom the wire dispatch called S. Missel and the Bodie Free Press called S. E. Mirales, a "countryman" of Salmon's. Salmon was arrested, and according to the dispatch the officers hid him "to preserve him from lynching." On Saturday his hiding place was discovered; the New-York Tribune's version of the telegram said instead that he was "taken out of prison," and a Minnesota brief said he was taken out of jail by a mob. He was hanged from the framework of a windmill at about ten o'clock that night.

The Austin Reveille, as reprinted by the Arizona Weekly Citizen, described the crowd halting and making a noose in wind and rain on a starless night. The Reese River Reveille attributed the hanging to a vigilance committee that signed itself "309," which also told another Mexican to leave Grantsville within twenty-four hours or face a "neck-tie party."

The Bodie Free Press said no particulars of the killing or the hanging had reached it, and no report of an inquest, of arrests of the lynchers, or of the fate of the second Mexican appears in the coverage.

Papers in the region endorsed the hanging, and the Gold Hill Daily News ran the Reese River Reveille's report under the headline "Judge Lynch at Grantsville." The Reveille said it was "to be regretted that lynch law has to be resorted to in a civilized country," but called it necessary "as a protection to life and property" and predicted that Grantsville would have no further trouble from "desperadoes." The Bodie Free Press reported that everybody in Bodie who knew Salmon "applauds the action of the people of Grantsville," and the Sacramento Daily Record-Union headed its reprint "Merited Fate" and "A 'Bad Man from Bodie' Executed by a Mob." Six weeks later the Arizona Weekly Citizen reprinted the Austin Reveille's florid description of the death of "a Mexican murderer," who went "unwept, unhonored and unsung."

Outside the region the story traveled as a three-sentence telegram dated February 5, which ran in the crime columns of the New-York Tribune, the Memphis Daily Appeal and the Chicago Daily Tribune on February 6. Their headlines were "Lynching a Murderer in Nevada," "Hunted and Hanged" and, in Chicago, "A Gentleman of Nevada," and the text called Salmon "a bad character." The dispatch reappeared over the following weeks in the Indiana State Sentinel, the Warren Sheaf (as "Matthews Salmon") and other papers. Weekly papers cut it to a single line, some dating the lynching "on the 5th."

The Reese River Reveille and the Bodie Free Press placed the hanging on Saturday night, the evening after the January 28 killing, and the Watertown Republican gave the date as January 29. Several weekly briefs instead dated it "on the 5th," apparently mistaking the date of the February 5 dispatch for the date of the lynching. Accounts also differ on whether Salmon was seized from an officers' hiding place or from a jail, and they spell both men's names, and the town's, in several ways.

bases: A man held for a killing was taken from officers' hiding place or jail and hanged by a vigilance committee or mob (A1, A3, A5, A6).

Salmon was hanged without lawful authority by a 'vigilance committee', 'the citizens' or 'a mob' (A1, A5, A6) after being accused of murder, and the papers presented it as summary justice (A1, A6); the victim was described as Mexican, not Black (A1, A6).
The Reese River Reveille (A1), the Bodie Free Press (A6), the Austin Reveille (A18) and the Feb. 5 telegraphic dispatch (A2, A3) independently report the hanging at Grantsville.
